conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, not a test of your parenting. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me there’s an immediate safety concern, and you can pause any time. We’ll walk through 10 gentle questions about the past seven days; just answer in your own words and we’ll figure the scoring together afterward. Ready to start?

Over the last week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

(soft half-laugh, then sighs)

Honestly… not very often. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I kind of chuckled for a second, but it faded fast. Most of the time things just feel heavy, like I’m too tired or worried to really find much funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I guess I can still laugh a little, but it’s pretty rare. Maybe once or twice in the past week I’ll catch myself smiling at something the baby does, or a text from a friend, but the feeling doesn’t last. Mostly I feel like I’m faking it or the laugh just dies in my throat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. Yesterday my husband asked if I wanted to watch our favorite show after the baby went down, and I said yes, but inside I felt… nothing. I sat through it without really caring what happened.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong,” or “She deserves a better mom.” Last night she wouldn’t latch, and I sat there crying, telling myself it was my fault for not trying harder. Rationally I know babies have off nights, but the guilt still barges in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly picture her blanket somehow covering her face, or worry the formula isn’t the right temperature, even though I just checked. My heart races and I can’t settle until I tiptoe in to watch her breathe—sometimes two or three times an hour. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just loop.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes... it hits out of nowhere. A couple nights ago I was warming a bottle in the kitchen and suddenly felt like I couldn't breathe—my chest got tight, the room felt too small, and I had to grip the counter. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky. And it keeps happening, maybe every other day, with no real trigger I can name.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most evenings. Things pile on each other—laundry, dishes, the baby’s next feed—and suddenly it feels like everything’s too much. Yesterday I snapped at my mom over nothing, then sat on the bed crying because I couldn’t find the right words.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… almost every night. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop replaying every little thing I might’ve messed up—did I wash the bottles right, is she breathing, am I already failing her. It takes me over an hour to drift off, and then I wake up two or three times with my heart pounding. By morning I feel like I’ve barely rested at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I feel that way most days. It’s like a gray cloud that hangs around even when the baby is smiling. I’ll be holding her and still feel this heaviness in my chest, like I’m stuck in a fog I can’t shake off.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week. Once was after her two-month shots—she cried, I cried, and I couldn’t stop. The other time I spilled some pumped milk and just sat on the floor sobbing, feeling like I’d ruined everything.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

(quiet voice, eyes on lap)

Once or twice… it’s more like a flash—what if I just kept driving past the house, or what if I didn’t wake up tomorrow. I’ve never made a plan or wanted to act on it; it’s just this quick, scary thought that pops in and then I push it away because I couldn’t leave her.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a persistent gray cloud: laughs fade quickly, pleasures feel like chores, and daily tasks pile up until they feel impossible. Despite loving your baby, you're carrying heavy <sym>guilt</sym>, nightly <sym>anxiety</sym> that keeps you awake, sudden <sym>panic</sym>, and occasional frightening <sym>self-harm flashes</sym> you would never act on. These feelings are valid, common, and treatable, and reaching out today is a courageous first step.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete absence of anticipatory enjoyment, even for previously pleasurable activities, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ('happens a lot,' 'I'm doing something wrong,' 'She deserves a better mom') matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, looping worries with physiological symptoms and compulsive checking, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks occurring frequently without identifiable triggers, matching 'Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('most evenings'), inability to manage tasks, emotional outbursts, and tearfulness, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption, racing thoughts, and repeated awakenings, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness ('most days'), pervasive gloom ('gray cloud'), and inability to feel joy even with baby, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring intrusive thoughts of self-harm (driving past, not waking up) but without intent or planning, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 plus Item 10 ≥1 mandates urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. Patient endorses <sym>low mood</sym> most days, marked <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia</sym>, <sym>recurrent panic</sym>, and <sym>self-harm cognitions</sym> consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. Functional impairment is evident; however, no active suicidal intent or plan is reported. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call 988 (U.S.) or your local crisis line if thoughts of not wanting to wake up become stronger or develop into an urge to self-harm
3. Begin basic <sym>sleep-hygiene</sym>: 20-min wind-down, low light, delegate one night-feed to partner or support person
4. Encourage 10-15 min daily gentle movement or outdoor stroller walk; sunlight can modestly lift mood
5. Reach out to a trusted friend/family each day for a 5-minute check-in-brief support reduces isolation
6. Consider PSI warm-line 1-800-944-4773 (or text 800-944-4773) for free 24/7 postpartum emotional support
7. Keep follow-up visit within one week to review screening, treatment options, and infant-feeding-compatible medications if indicated
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening note – Postpartum visit

Symptoms endorsed
- Persistent low mood, sadness “most days”
- Marked loss of interest/pleasure in previously enjoyed activities
- Daily guilt/self-blame (“bad mother” cognitions)
- Frequent crying spells, difficulty controlling emotions
- Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, middle-of-night anxious awakenings)
- Recurrent intrusive worries about infant’s safety; panic-like episodes
- Feeling overwhelmed, difficulty coping with routine tasks
- Passive self-harm ideation without plan (fleeting thoughts of “not waking up,” driving past house)

Patterns/risk indicators
Consistent with probable depressive and anxiety symptoms starting postpartum; functional impairment evident. Passive suicidal ideation present → safety screening warranted.

Screening significance
Elevated likelihood of major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder. No active suicidal intent reported; continue suicide-risk monitoring.

Next step
Urgent referral for formal diagnostic evaluation and safety plan.
